meta.titre: Protein Synthesis: Transcription, the Genetic Code and Translation

sections.contenu_markdown: Every plate of ndole or eru you eat is mostly protein, and your body must rebuild all of it into the thousands of different proteins that make your muscles, enzymes, haemoglobin and antibodies. The instructions are stored in DNA in the nucleus, but the proteins are built at ribosomes in the cytoplasm, so a messenger has to carry the information from one place to the other. Protein synthesis is tested every year in multiple choice questions on the genetic code, on the roles of the different kinds of RNA, and on calculations linking the number of amino acids to the number of nucleotides. If you master the vocabulary and the steps, these become fast marks.

items: DNA is made of nucleotides containing the bases adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine; RNA contains uracil in place of thymine and ribose in place of deoxyribose.
A protein is a polymer of amino acids joined by peptide bonds, and a gene is the section of DNA that carries the code for one polypeptide.
Ribosomes are made of ribosomal RNA and protein and are found free in the cytoplasm and attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
Complementary base pairing joins A with T (or U in RNA) and C with G.

sections.titre: From gene to polypeptide: transcription, the genetic code and translation
sections.contenu_markdown:
**The genetic code.** A sequence of three bases is a **codon** (in mRNA) and codes for one amino acid. The code is a **triplet code**, **non-overlapping**, **degenerate** (most amino acids have more than one codon, so there are 64 codons for 20 amino acids), **universal** (almost the same in all organisms) and contains a **start codon** AUG (methionine) and three **stop codons** (UAA, UAG, UGA) that code for no amino acid. The sequence of bases in DNA therefore determines the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide.

**Transcription** (in the nucleus). The enzyme **RNA polymerase** attaches to a promoter at the start of the gene, and the DNA unwinds. One strand, the **template (antisense) strand**, is used. Free ribonucleotides pair with the exposed bases (A with U, T with A, C with G, G with C) and are joined to make a strand of **mRNA** that grows from its 5' end to its 3' end. The mRNA has the same base sequence as the other (coding or sense) strand, with U in place of T. In eukaryotes the pre-mRNA is processed: introns are removed, exons are joined (splicing), and a cap and a tail are added before the mRNA leaves through a nuclear pore.

**Translation** (at the ribosome, in the cytoplasm). **tRNA** molecules are folded into a clover-leaf shape with an **anticodon** at one end and an amino acid binding site at the other. An enzyme attaches each tRNA to its specific amino acid using energy from ATP. The small ribosomal subunit binds the mRNA at the start codon AUG, and the tRNA with the anticodon UAC carrying methionine pairs with it. The large subunit joins, and a second tRNA binds to the next codon. A peptide bond forms between the two amino acids (a condensation reaction), the ribosome moves along the mRNA by one codon, and the first tRNA leaves. This repeats until a stop codon is reached; no tRNA matches a stop codon, so a release factor binds, and the **polypeptide** is released. The end product of translation is a polypeptide, which then folds and may be modified in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus.

**Counting.** A polypeptide of n amino acids needs a coding sequence of 3n nucleotides, or 3(n + 1) if the stop codon is counted; it forms (n - 1) peptide bonds.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Use when a question changes, adds or removes a base and asks what happens to the polypeptide.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
A **gene mutation** is a change in the base sequence of DNA.

| Type | Change | Effect on the polypeptide |
|---|---|---|
| Substitution, silent | One base replaced and the new codon codes for the same amino acid | No change (the code is degenerate) |
| Substitution, missense | New codon codes for a different amino acid | One amino acid changes |
| Substitution, nonsense | New codon is a stop codon | Polypeptide cut short |
| Insertion or deletion (not a multiple of three) | Reading frame shifts | All amino acids after the change are altered (frameshift) |

Example: in sickle-cell haemoglobin the codon GAG (glutamic acid) becomes GUG (valine) in the mRNA, because of one base substitution in the DNA, giving a different haemoglobin that polymerises at low oxygen.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Use when a question asks for the structure or role of each RNA, or for the difference between a codon and an anticodon.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
| Feature | mRNA | tRNA | rRNA |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shape | Single, linear strand | Clover-leaf with a loop containing the anticodon | Folded, part of ribosome subunits |
| Made in | Nucleus (transcription) | Nucleus (from genes) | Nucleolus |
| Role | Carries the code (codons) from DNA to the ribosome | Brings a specific amino acid to its codon by its anticodon | Forms the ribosome with protein; catalyses peptide bond formation |
| Sequence | Complementary to the template strand | Anticodon complementary to a codon | Not read as a code |

sections.enonce_markdown:
Part of the template strand of a gene is written 3'-TACCGATTTCTTGGAACCACT-5'. The codons needed are given in the table.

| Codon | Amino acid |
|---|---|
| AUG | Met |
| GCU | Ala |
| AAA | Lys |
| GAA | Glu |
| CCU | Pro |
| UGG | Trp |
| UGA | Stop (no amino acid) |

(a) Write the base sequence of the mRNA transcribed from this strand, labelled 5' to 3'. (b) Write the anticodon of the tRNA that pairs with the first codon. (c) State the order of amino acids in the polypeptide. (d) Explain why the polypeptide is shorter than the number of codons.

etapes.action: Pair each base of the template strand with its RNA partner.
etapes.justification: RNA polymerase builds mRNA complementary to the template strand: T pairs with A, A with U, C with G and G with C. The template is written 3' to 5', so the mRNA comes out written 5' to 3'.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Template 3'-TAC CGA TTT CTT GGA ACC ACT-5' gives mRNA 5'-**AUG GCU AAA GAA CCU UGG UGA**-3'.

etapes.action: Check the answer against the coding strand.
etapes.justification: The mRNA must have the same sequence as the coding strand with U in place of T.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Coding strand 5'-ATGGCTAAAGAACCTTGGTGA-3' becomes AUGGCUAAAGAACCUUGGUGA when T is replaced by U, which matches.

etapes.action: Find the anticodon for the first codon AUG.
etapes.justification: The anticodon is complementary and antiparallel to the codon.

etapes.action: Translate codon by codon using the table.
etapes.justification: Each codon codes for one amino acid until a stop codon is reached.
etapes.resultat_markdown: AUG = Met, GCU = Ala, AAA = Lys, GAA = Glu, CCU = Pro, UGG = Trp, UGA = Stop. Sequence: **Met - Ala - Lys - Glu - Pro - Trp**.

etapes.justification: A stop codon has no matching tRNA, so it is not translated into an amino acid.
etapes.resultat_markdown: There are 7 codons but the last (UGA) is a stop codon, so the polypeptide has **6 amino acids**.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The mRNA is 5'-AUGGCUAAAGAACCUUGGUGA-3'; the first anticodon is UAC; the polypeptide is Met-Ala-Lys-Glu-Pro-Trp. Seven codons code for six amino acids because the stop codon codes for nothing.

items.pourquoi_faux: Thymine is found only in DNA. In RNA the base uracil takes its place and pairs with adenine.
items.correction_markdown: In mRNA the bases are A, U, C and G; wherever the template has A, the mRNA has U.

items.erreur_markdown: "The tRNA carries the codon and the mRNA carries the anticodon."
items.pourquoi_faux: The terms are swapped. The mRNA is read in codons, while each tRNA has an anticodon that pairs with a codon.

items.erreur_markdown: "The mRNA is complementary to the coding strand."
items.pourquoi_faux: The mRNA is made on the template strand, so it is complementary to the template strand. It is identical to the coding strand except that U replaces T.
items.correction_markdown: mRNA = complementary to the **template** strand = same sequence as the **coding** strand (with U).

items.erreur_markdown: "A polypeptide of 100 amino acids needs 100 nucleotides in its gene."
items.pourquoi_faux: One amino acid is coded by a codon of three nucleotides, so the number of nucleotides is three times the number of amino acids.
items.correction_markdown: 100 amino acids need **300 nucleotides** (303 if the stop codon is included).

items.erreur_markdown: "Translation takes place in the nucleus and transcription in the cytoplasm."
items.pourquoi_faux: Transcription copies DNA, which stays in the nucleus. Translation needs ribosomes, which are in the cytoplasm or on the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
items.correction_markdown: **Transcription in the nucleus; translation at ribosomes** in the cytoplasm.

items.enonce_markdown:
A short section of the template strand of a gene is 3'-TACAAACCGGTTATT-5'.

| Codon | Amino acid |
|---|---|
| AUG | Met |
| UUU | Phe |
| GGC | Gly |
| CAA | Gln |
| UAA | Stop |

(a) Write the mRNA sequence from 5' to 3'. (b) Write the anticodons of the tRNA molecules that pair with each codon. (c) State the amino acid sequence.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Complement each base of the template: mRNA 5'-**AUG UUU GGC CAA UAA**-3'.

(b) Anticodons (3' to 5'): UAC, AAA, CCG, GUU; the final codon UAA is a stop codon, so no tRNA matches it.

(c) AUG = Met, UUU = Phe, GGC = Gly, CAA = Gln, UAA = Stop. The polypeptide is **Met - Phe - Gly - Gln** (4 amino acids).

(a) 85 × 3 = **255 nucleotides**.

(b) One extra codon for the stop signal: 86 × 3 = **258 nucleotides**.

(c) Joining 85 amino acids needs 85 - 1 = **84 peptide bonds**.

(d) Each mRNA nucleotide corresponds to one base pair of the gene, so **258 base pairs**.

items.enonce_markdown:
The mRNA for a short peptide is 5'-AUGGAACUUAAAGGCUGA-3'. Use the table.

| Codon | Amino acid |
|---|---|
| AUG | Met |
| GAA | Glu |
| GAG | Glu |
| CUU | Leu |
| AAA | Lys |
| AAG | Lys |
| GGC | Gly |
| GCU | Ala |
| UAA | Stop |
| UGA | Stop |

(a) Give the amino acid sequence of the normal peptide. (b) Mutation 1: the third base of codon 2 changes from A to G. Mutation 2: the first base of codon 2 changes from G to U. Mutation 3: the first A of codon 4 is deleted. Work out the effect of each mutation on the peptide. (c) Which mutation is likely to have the most serious effect? Explain.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Met - Glu - Leu - Lys - Gly (the codon UGA is a stop codon).

(b) Mutation 1 changes GAA to GAG. Both code for Glu, so the peptide is unchanged (Met - Glu - Leu - Lys - Gly): a **silent** substitution because the code is degenerate.

Mutation 2 changes GAA to UAA, a stop codon, so the peptide is **Met only**: a **nonsense** mutation.

Mutation 3 removes one base, so the sequence after the deletion is read in a new frame: AUG GAA CUU AAG GCU GA. The peptide is **Met - Glu - Leu - Lys - Ala**, the fifth amino acid is Ala instead of Gly, and the stop codon is lost, so the ribosome would continue reading beyond this region: a **frameshift** mutation.

(c) The nonsense mutation (peptide cut to a single amino acid, almost certainly non-functional) and the frameshift mutation (altered amino acids and loss of the stop signal) are the most serious. The silent mutation has no effect.

items_markdown: The genetic code is a triplet, non-overlapping, degenerate and universal code; AUG is the start codon and UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons.
Transcription: RNA polymerase makes mRNA complementary to the template strand in the nucleus; mRNA has the same sequence as the coding strand with U for T.
Translation: mRNA is read at a ribosome; tRNA anticodons pair with codons, and peptide bonds form between the amino acids until a stop codon releases the polypeptide.
The end products of translation are polypeptides; mRNA is made in transcription.
n amino acids need 3n nucleotides (3n + 3 with the stop codon) and form n - 1 peptide bonds.
Substitutions can be silent, missense or nonsense; insertions and deletions that are not multiples of three cause frameshifts.
